title: Python GC pause latency log (scratch)
content:
Context:
Small, informal log capturing a recurring ~10-60ms spike in token emit latency that I think maps to Python GC activity inside the request handling path (we're using a thin Python RPC worker that wraps the C++ inference core). This is a personal scratchpad — experiments, CLI commands, traces and quick hypotheses.

Setup summary (baseline harness):
- Model: opt-1.3b-like local build (quantized toy model) running on single GPU node.
- Serving binary: compiled C++ engine (fastpath) + Python worker process that receives requests, merges headers, calls into C++ via pybind11.
- Load generator: rps-probe (locally written) with deterministic arrivals; test script attached in linked_artifacts.
- Workload: 64-token generations, batch size 1, concurrency 8, QPS sweep [5, 20, 50].
- Env: Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11, GENV venv, jemalloc disabled, GC thresholds default.

Observation timeline (first 3 runs):
1) 2025-11-08 09:12 — QPS 20, p50 ~18ms, p95 ~32ms, p99 ~68ms. Spikes appear as isolated events every ~6–18s.
2) 2025-11-09 14:05 — Increased concurrency to 16, p99 jumps to 120ms with same pattern; trace shows a ~30–60ms pause in Python thread during completion callback.
3) 2025-11-10 11:20 — Disabled GC (gc.disable()) in worker main loop: spikes mostly disappear, p99 reduces to ~38ms.

Hypothesis:
- The Python worker allocates short-lived objects per request (metadata dicts, temporary tensors views, callback closures). Periodic GC cycles introduce stop-the-world pauses in the worker thread and therefore add tail latency to the token emit path. Because the C++ engine returns quickly, the Python layer's callback pause directly shows up in end-to-end latency.

Quick experiments and commands run:
- baseline run (collect flamegraphs):
  $ perf record -F 99 -g -- python worker_entry.py --bench qps=20 --concurrency=8
  $ perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; flamegraph.pl out.folded > baseline.svg
- live GC toggle (debug harness): added a small wrapper that calls gc.disable() for the inner request loop and gc.enable() on graceful shutdown.
- incremental GC tuning: set gc.set_threshold(700, 10, 10) and rerun.
- object allocation sampling: added tracemalloc snapshot at start and after 10k requests.

Results (notes):
- gc.disable(): immediate reduction of periodic ~30–60ms spikes. However, memory climbs steadily (expected) — not acceptable long term without alternate memory reclamation.
- raising thresholds to (700, 10, 10): reduced spike frequency by ~60% at QPS 20; p99 moved from 68ms -> ~46ms.
- tracemalloc shows many short-lived dicts sized ~300–2kB per request, primarily headers + token-merge temporary.

Micro-trace extract (sampled):
- spike event at 2025-11-09T14:05:23.125Z
  - Python: GC collect -> 42ms total
  - C++: waiting on callback -> 42ms blocked on Python GIL
  - rps-probe: observed client RTT bump aligned with above timestamp

Potential mitigations to test (ranked):
1) Move hot-path code out of Python: minimize allocations in callback by preallocating small reusable objects (small object pool) or pushing more logic into C++ callback. Low-risk, medium effort.
2) Switch to incremental/trash-avoiding patterns: reuse dicts, pre-allocate bytearrays for headers. Low effort per-PR, should shave many small allocations.
3) Fine-tune Python GC thresholds for prod worker processes (per-process tuning on startup based on observed allocation rate). Medium risk (must guard memory growth).
4) Offload callback handling to dedicated thread/process so GC pauses don't block critical token emitter (introduces IPC latency/complexity). Higher complexity.
5) Replace Python worker with lightweight Rust wrapper that calls into C++ engine (major work).

Next quick experiments (to run):
- A: Implement small object pool for request-metadata (POC branch: samira/gc-pool). Measure p99 at QPS 50.
- B: Add per-request GC suppression: call gc.disable() briefly during the actual token emit and re-enable after. Danger: race with background threads; but may reduce spikes.
- C: Run jemalloc on Python process + tune GC thresholds: track RSS over 30m to confirm safe memory.
- D: Evaluate PyPy for worker — interesting because of different GC semantics; run quick perf smoke.

Open questions / notes:
- Are we seeing any correlation with minor vs major GC? Need to instrument gc.get_count() and gc.callbacks to classify.
- Compare with purely C++ path (no Python worker) to quantify absolute delta. I have a C++-only harness in linked_artifacts PR 1423 — ideally rerun same QPS/concurrency.
- Validate whether GIL acquisition time is the main blocker or whether syscalls in GC path (e.g., malloc) re-enter C++.

Raw numbers summary (QPS 20, concurrency 8):
- baseline: p50 18ms, p95 32ms, p99 68ms, mem RSS 420MB
- gc.disable toggle: p50 16ms, p95 20ms, p99 38ms, mem RSS climbs ~+30MB per 10k reqs
- thresholds(700): p50 18ms, p95 28ms, p99 46ms, mem RSS stable

Quick action items I will do next (short):
- Push small object-pool POC branch (samira/gc-pool) — today.
- Add lightweight GC metrics to telemetry (gc_count/minor/major, gc_pause_ms histogram) — file a ticket JIRA-INF-824.
- Re-run perf with jemalloc vs system malloc to check allocation pause behavior.

Notes to reviewers: this is a handwritten scratchpad — if you see this and have prior art (runtime team tweaks, patterns we already use in dedicated workers), ping me so I don't duplicate work. The immediate win likely comes from allocation reduction + GC threshold tuning rather than full rewrite.

End of log.
